An important thing you need to know is that not only one particle can behave like a wave. A group of particle can behave as a wave too. When one particle behaves as a wave, there is a wave like probability of where it is. When many behave as a wave, there is a probability for every combination of positions of the particles.

When particles interact their states become correlated. One example of this could be that we know that either both particles are in one place or none are. When a particle goes through the double slit and hit the detector behind it that is exactly what happens. Either the particle is in one place, and the detector detects it there, or it is in another place and the detector detects it there or a third place...

It is this process of creating a correlation with a macroscopic system that we call observation.

Note that at no point does the uncertainty actually vanish. It is just moved to a bigger system. What would happen if the measurement device becomes correlated with the state of the particle, but the device itself is kept in an isolated box away from the experimenter? Then in principle the device itself will be in several states at once from the perspective of the experimenter. This means that it can interfere with itself, just like the particle going through both slits could interfere with itself.
